🐦

Your WordPress Early-Warning System

WP Canary watches your site overnight and tells you exactly what broke — before your customers notice.

Get WP Canary — $39
See Free Features →

Sound familiar?

😫

You wake up to a broken site and have no idea what happened overnight.

🔌

Plugins mysteriously deactivate and you only find out from an angry customer.

📜

Your debug log is a wall of noise and you can’t tell what’s actually wrong.

Everything you need to catch problems before they become disasters

🗄️

Database Table Scanner

Checks WooCommerce, Yoast, Redirection, and Contact Form 7 tables for missing columns and broken schemas. One-click repair with admin confirmation.

🔌

Plugin Status Watchdog

Monitors your active plugins every 15 minutes and alerts you the moment anything deactivates unexpectedly. Keeps a 30-day history of every change.

🚫

404 Flood Detector

Identifies IPs and bots generating abnormal 404 traffic. Flags when the flood is causing database stress and suggests exactly what to do.

📢

Ad Network Monitor

Detects Google, Meta, and Bing ad bots hitting your site off-hours and identifies when they’re triggering unexpected cron jobs or plugin conflicts.

📋

Debug Log Analyzer

Filters out harmless noise and surfaces only actionable errors in plain English. Groups repeated errors and identifies which plugin caused each one.

☀️

Morning Email Digest

Get a plain-English summary of overnight activity delivered to your inbox every morning. Separate technical detail section for developers.

🐘

PHP Resource Monitor

Tracks memory limits, peak usage, and execution timeouts. Alerts you before resource exhaustion takes your site down.

⏰

WP-Cron Health Monitor

Detects missed and late cron jobs. Flags unreliable WP-Cron on low-traffic sites and recommends switching to real server cron.

Frequently asked questions

Does WP Canary slow down my site?

No. All scans run during low-traffic windows using WP-Cron. The 404 monitor adds a negligible hook on 404 pages only.

Will it conflict with Wordfence or Sucuri?

WP Canary is designed to operate in read-mostly mode. All write operations require explicit admin confirmation so security plugins don’t flag it.

What happens after the first year on the one-time plan?

The plugin keeps working forever. You just won’t receive new feature updates or support after year one unless you renew.

Does it work on WordPress Multisite?

Yes. WP Canary is network-activated and managed from the network admin by the super admin.

Which hosts is it compatible with?

Tested on A2 Hosting, WP Engine, SiteGround, Kinsta, and Bluehost. No external API dependencies — everything runs locally.

Stop finding out about problems from your customers

Join site owners who get their morning digest instead of morning panic.

Privacy Policy

Last updated: June 7, 2026

WP Canary (getwpcanary.com) respects your privacy. This policy explains what data we collect, how we use it, and your rights regarding that data.

Data Collection

The WP Canary plugin operates entirely locally on your WordPress installation. No site data is transmitted to our servers. When you purchase a Pro license via Freemius, your name and email address are processed by Freemius under their privacy policy.

Contact

For privacy questions, contact us at privacy@getwpcanary.com.

item.title: Why WordPress Plugins Mysteriously Deactivate (And How to Catch It)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
You log into your WordPress admin on a Tuesday morning and notice your WooCommerce store stopped processing payments some time the previous night. The culprit? A plugin silently deactivated itself, and nobody — not you, not your customers (well, except for the angry ones) — knew about it until the damage was done.

Plugin deactivation is one of the sneakiest problems in WordPress because there is no built-in notification system. WordPress simply deactivates a plugin and moves on, leaving you to discover the gap on your own. But why does it happen in the first place?

The Most Common Causes

1. Hosting Timeouts During Updates

When WordPress runs a plugin update, it temporarily deactivates the plugin, swaps out the files, then reactivates it. If your server has a tight PHP execution time limit (common on shared hosts) and the file swap takes too long, the process dies mid-update. The plugin is left deactivated because the reactivation step never ran.

2. PHP Fatal Errors on Activation

WordPress has a self-protection mechanism: if a plugin throws a PHP fatal error, WordPress deactivates it to prevent a complete site crash. This is a good safety feature, but it means a bad plugin update or a PHP version incompatibility can silently kill a plugin you depend on. The error gets logged (if debug logging is enabled), but nothing tells you the plugin is gone.

3. Database Errors During Plugin Operations

Some plugins write to the database during activation and deactivation hooks. If a database table is missing a column, if the database server is under load, or if a transaction fails, the operation can leave the plugin in an undefined state. You might see a plugin listed as active in the database but not actually functioning, or vice versa.

4. WP-Cron Failures and Timing Issues

WP-Cron is notoriously unreliable on low-traffic sites. If a scheduled maintenance task that includes plugin management runs at an unexpected time, or if a cron job fires twice due to a missed previous run, it can interfere with plugin state. This is especially common on sites that rely on WP-Cron for auto-updates.

How to Catch It Before Your Customers Do

The fundamental problem is that WordPress does not offer any native alerting for plugin state changes. The best you can do manually is check your plugins screen regularly, which is not realistic at 3 AM when most deactivations happen during overnight maintenance windows.

This is exactly the problem that WP Canary’s Plugin Status Watchdog was built to solve. It polls your active plugin list every 15 minutes using WP-Cron, compares it against a stored baseline, and immediately triggers an email alert if anything changes. It also maintains a 30-day changelog of every activation and deactivation event, so when something breaks you can see exactly what changed and when, rather than guessing.

Combined with WP Canary’s Morning Email Digest, you get a daily summary of any plugin state changes that occurred overnight, alongside your debug log summary, PHP resource usage, and cron job health. It is not a substitute for a proper staging environment and careful update process, but it is a reliable safety net for the unexpected things that happen on production sites at inconvenient hours.

If you have ever been the last person to know your site was broken, that is the problem WP Canary is here to fix.
